Issued at 223 AM CDT Sun Jul 26 2026

Synopsis:

A strong mid-upper level ridge over the central-southern Plains
into the southwest U.S. is progged to weaken slightly and
retrograde west a bit through the middle of the upcoming work
week. Meanwhile, mid-upper level troughing will amplifying over
the northeast U.S. through midweek, with our area locked in
northwest flow much of the upcoming work week. Our CWA will be
on the edge of the heat and humidity and strong instability,
leaving us prone to convection until a cold front moves across
the area Monday evening, ushering in a much less humid and more
stable air mass for much of the upcoming work week. 

Today: 

While a much more humid air mass is expected to expand/spread
northeast into our area today, there is some uncertainty
regarding temperatures. Tossing out the too deeply mixed HRRR
and RRFS, that leaves most guidance suggesting a stout low 
level inversion will persist today. Despite the high July sun 
angle, the stratus beneath the low level inversion may be a bit
slow to break up this morning. In addition to the potential for
lingering low cloudiness, considerable mid-high level 
cloudiness (especially this morning) is expected as remnants of 
the earlier SD MCS move across the area. Assuming we get some 
mixed sunshine this afternoon, which seems to be a reasonable 
assumption, then high temps reaching the upper 80s to lower 90s 
looks reasonable. Dewpoints climbing into the mid to perhaps 
upper 70s over our western/southwestern CWA this afternoon 
should push heat indices above 100 to perhaps locally around 105
degrees, so no changes planned to the heat advisory.

Other than the models that are too "mixy" there is a pretty good
consensus that atmosphere will remain capped today. There's
likely a weak remnant MCV with the decayed MCS over IA/MN, but
this feature is likely to pass to our west and likely be south
of our area before it would have a better chance of sparking
renewed convection this afternoon. Overall, precip chances
during the daytime hours look to be less than 15% and plan to
stick with a dry forecast for today. 

Tonight through Monday:

The early evening hours should be dry (precipitation-wise), but
quite warm and humid. Focus for convective potential tonight is
on shortwave trough evident on water vapor imagery from eastern
MT north into southern Saskatchewan. Initialization of this 
fairly subtle shortwave varies among the various models and 
unsurprisingly leads to a wide array of possible solutions. 
Extrapolation would favor this wave cresting the upper ridge 
this morning and probably resulting in convective initiation 
over northeastern MN or northern WI later this afternoon. 
Certainly possible that this convection could congeal into an 
MCS this evening, but there is uncertainty whether that 
evolution into an MCS takes place and if it does, exactly where.

If there is an MCS over northern WI early this evening, forward
propagating Corfidi Vectors, 850-300 mb thickness, and the
orientation of the instability axis would all support an MCS
moving southeast and then southward overnight. A 40kt low level
jet could help maintain an MCS southward into northern IL or
northern IN late tonight or early Monday morning. While there is
considerable spread in the timing, the 00z GFS, RGEM, and ECMWF
all have a nice convective QPF signal into northern IL tonight 
or Monday morning. The stronger effective deep layer shear
tonight should be north of our CWA across the upper Great Lakes,
but there should be enough mid level flow to support an MCS
getting into our area, possibly in a weakening phase absent the
development of a parent MCV to augment shear. Given the
magnitude of instability, potential would certainly exist for
damaging winds, should a well developed MCS make it into our 
area tonight or Monday morning. 

Already low forecast confidence gets even lower (if that is
possible) for Monday afternoon and evening. If we dodge having
an MCS roll through here Monday morning, then all systems would
be go for a oppressively hot and humid day Monday with heat
indices 100F to locally over 110F in the areas with the most
extreme evapotranspiration and likely lower 80 degree dewpoints.
If there is an MCS, then temps Monday will hinge on timing of 
it moving out, how big of a cold pool footprint is left behind, 
how much cloudiness lingers. With confidence low, but increasing
a bit in a potential MCS in the neighborhood late tonight or
Monday morning, confidence in dangerous heat Monday is a bit
lower. Given this, nudged forecast high temps down a bit from
the NBM, but potentially still way too hot if an MCS does
significantly alter the thermal fields. If confidence increases
that convection won't prohibit the heat, then Monday may well
end up needed heat headlines, but for now, a wait and see
approach seems to be the most prudent way to go.
